note: Band recipes (nebulae-and-light design 2.2). Data only: a pack can add more. Each says what its colours mean and how honest they are.

recipes.name: Eye
recipes.legend: What a person would see: each mark takes the colour of its light through the CIE 1931 standard observer, shown on an sRGB screen.
recipes.why: Colour matching functions turn a spectrum into the three numbers an eye sends the brain. Wyman, Sloan and Shirley's fit of the CIE 1931 functions (JCGT 2(2), 2013, http://jcgt.org/published/0002/02/01/) and the sRGB standard (IEC 61966-2-1) do the rest.

recipes.name: Camera
recipes.legend: A colour camera's three broad filters, white-balanced to daylight, with saturation raised as a press photograph would be. Real light, stronger colour than the eye sees.
recipes.why: Cameras sample light through red, green and blue filters that do not match the eye's response, and published pictures are usually stretched. This recipe does both, and says so.

recipes.name: Hubble palette (SHO)
recipes.legend: Narrowband light from sulphur, hydrogen and oxygen painted red, green and blue. The colours label chemistry; they are not what an eye sees.
recipes.why: The palette the Hubble team used for the Pillars of Creation (1995). Each filter passes a few nanometres around one emission line. Bodies with no line emission show only the continuum under the filters.

recipes.name: Bicolour (HOO)
recipes.legend: Hydrogen-alpha painted red and doubly ionised oxygen painted cyan, the amateur bicolour palette. Mapped colour.
recipes.why: Two narrowband filters cover the brightest lines of most emission nebulae, which is why amateurs with mono cameras use this pair.

recipes.name: Near infrared
recipes.legend: Brightness in the near infrared, faint to bright along an amber ramp across eight decades. One band shown as one colour: mapped.
recipes.why: Near-infrared light passes through dust that hides visible light, and cool stars are brightest here.

recipes.name: Thermal infrared
recipes.legend: Brightness in the mid infrared, where worlds glow by their own heat. Faint to bright along a red ramp across six decades. Mapped.
recipes.why: A world at a few hundred kelvin gives off most of its light near 10 µm (Wien's law), so here planets shine by their own warmth, not by reflected starlight.

recipes.name: Ultraviolet
recipes.legend: Brightness in the ultraviolet along a violet ramp across ten decades. Mapped.
recipes.why: Hot stars are bright in the ultraviolet; cool stars and planets barely show. Stellar activity, which makes cool stars bright here, is not modelled yet.

recipes.name: X-ray
recipes.legend: Brightness in X-rays along a blue ramp. With only thermal light modelled, almost nothing here shows: real stars are lit by hot coronae, which arrive with stellar activity.
recipes.why: A blackbody at a star's surface temperature gives off essentially no X-rays. The dark view is the honest answer until coronae are modelled.

recipes.name: Radio
recipes.legend: Thermal radio brightness along a green ramp across six decades. Mapped. Synchrotron and auroral radio are not modelled yet.
recipes.why: In the Rayleigh-Jeans tail, thermal radio brightness grows only in step with temperature, so warm planets come much closer to their star here than in visible light.
